extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators and IPR practitioners (parties before the PTAB, counsel handling inter partes reviews)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for litigants and counsel on how the PTAB treats prior district-court or ITC claim constructions in IPRs and strategies to reinforce, undermine, or avoid those prior constructions. Covers the factors the PTAB weighs and practical briefing/record-building tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB factors for weighing prior constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB considers exemplary factors in determining the 'appropriate weight' to give a prior claim construction: (1) the similarities between the record in the district court or the ITC and the record before the Board; (2) whether the prior claim construction is final or interlocutory; (3) whether the terms construed by the district court or ITC are necessary to deciding the issues before it; and (4) the facts and circumstances of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source: Patent Trial and Appeal Board Consolidated Trial Practice Guide (Trial Practice Guide) at 47 (Nov. 2019). These factors should be addressed in briefing to explain why a prior construction should or should not be given weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and predictability concern
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB is concerned that inconsistent claim constructions across tribunals would 'undermine the
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTAB has repeatedly stated that lack of uniformity would undermine a patent's predictability and 'the integrity of the patent system' overall; arguing for consistency (or against it) should address this policy concern. Examples: Kiosoft Techs. v. PayRange; Google v. Virentem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight given when parties do not dispute prior constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: When neither party challenges a prior construction, or parties advocating alternatives fail to support them, the PTAB is particularly reticent to depart from that prior construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where PTAB adopted prior constructions for this reason: Google LLC v. Uniloc 2017 LLC (neither party challenged Texas court construction); 3Shape A/S v. Align Tech., Inc. (adopted ITC constructions where Patent Owner provided no contrary evidence). Parties seeking to change a prior construction must expressly challenge and support departure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on party proposing an alternative construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A party advocating a construction that differs from one adopted by a district court or the ITC must 'explain why [the PTAB] should depart from those constructions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere adoption of a different construction is insufficient; the proponent must identify flaws in the prior reasoning or present intrinsic/extrinsic evidence the earlier tribunal overlooked. Failure to do so can result in denial of institution or failure to show likelihood of prevailing (see OrthoPediatrics v. K2M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attack weaknesses or absence of reasoning in prior constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and attack weaknesses in the reasoning behind a prior construction (or point out that there was no reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the district court provided little or no explanation (e.g., simply 'plain and ordinary meaning'), the PTAB may give it little weight or supply a more detailed construction. Example: Micron Tech., Inc. v. Godo Kaisha IP Bridge 1 (deviated where district court lacked reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intrinsic and extrinsic evidence to support departure or adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Accentuate helpful intrinsic and extrinsic evidence (specification, prosecution history, expert testimony, dictionaries) that the district court or the ITC may have ignored or given short shrift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB applies Phillips: consider claim language, specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence. Where the PTAB endorses a prior construction it often quotes and adopts the prior tribunal's reasoning or independently examines the specification and experts (e.g., MediaTek v. NTT; Lab. Corp. v. Quest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor arguments to claim construction canons (first principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments should be grounded in basic canons of claim construction: consistency with claim language and specification, avoidance of importing limitations from the specification, and not excluding preferred/claimed embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB 'departs' from prior constructions that violate basic rules (e.g., importing limitations or creating redundancy). Demonstrating that a prior construction contradicts these tenets is an effective way to evade it; showing compliance helps secure adoption (see Juniper Networks v. Packet Intel; Renesas v. Broadcom). File history arguments may be persuasive given PTAB expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare the records across proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of similarity or difference between the record that produced the prior construction and the IPR record affects the PTAB's weight assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the IPR record and arguments are the same as in the prior forum, emphasize that sameness to support adoption. If they differ (additional evidence, different expert testimony, deposition contradictions), emphasize those differences to justify departure. Example: Virentem (PTAB departed due to different records and contested construction in IPR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of detail in prior decision matters
rubrics_metrics.description: If a district court's construction lacks opinion, reasoning, or explanation (or just adopts 'plain and ordinary meaning' without elaboration), the PTAB will give it less weight and may provide its own detailed construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB has supplied more detailed constructions where prior tribunals offered only 'plain and ordinary meaning' (e.g., Micron Tech. v. Unification Techs.; Bumble Trading v. Match). Parties should point out paucity of reasoning to justify PTAB reanalysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB may adopt prior constructions after endorsing their reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB sometimes quotes a district court's or ITC's reasoning, finds it persuasive, and adopts the same construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the PTAB 'finds this reasoning persuasive,' it may adopt the prior construction (examples: Google v. Virentem; Bayerische Motoren Werke v. Paice). Demonstrating strong, reasoned prior analysis increases likelihood of adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB is not bound by prior constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior constructions from other courts based on the Phillips standard do not bind the PTAB; the PTAB can and has found prior constructions wanting and adopted different constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB will deviate when prior constructions violate claim construction rules, import limitations, exclude embodiments, or are otherwise flawed (examples: Juniper Networks; Renesas). Emphasize such flaws if seeking deviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality/affirmation increases weight
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior construction is final or has been affirmed by an appellate court (e.g., Federal Circuit), the PTAB may feel 'compelled' to construe consistently with that construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affirmed district-court construction carries significant persuasive force (example: Ford Motor Co. v. MIT, where PTAB felt compelled to be consistent with a Federal Circuit-affirmed construction). Note this is a factor, not an absolute binding rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB can decline to construe terms unnecessary to resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB often concludes that interpreting previously construed terms is unnecessary to resolving the dispute and therefore avoids adopting or rejecting prior constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the Trial Practice Guide's permissive language: PTAB considers whether construing terms is 'necessary to deciding the issues before it.' Examples: Huawei v. WSOU; Ability Opto-Electronics v. Largan; LG Elecs. v. Cywee. Parties can strategically argue that construction is unnecessary to keep PTAB from addressing a prior (favorable) construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions may be preliminary and open to continued briefing
rubrics_metrics.description: When the PTAB adopts or departs from a prior construction, it sometimes underscores that its construction is preliminary and invites the parties to provide additional arguments during the IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB may adopt a construction 'for purposes of this Decision as our preliminary construction' and invite further briefing (see Semiconductor Components IPR2018-01811; Unification IPR2021-00345). Parties should be prepared to refine arguments at institution and in later phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic briefing: address all proposed and existing constructions relative to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should explain how the prior art reads on the challenged claims 'under all proposed and existing constructions' because failing to address alternative constructions risks losing the chance to advocate under a less favorable construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if advocating an alternative, show analyses under the prior construction as well. The PTAB will consider prior constructions, so comprehensive prior-art application across constructions strengthens a party's position.
